title: Cells: The Basic Units of Life

scenes.visual: Title: "Cells: The Basic Units of Life". Show a plant, an animal and a bacterium, with cells highlighted. No historical date or tool-first question.

scenes.tts: Every living organism is made of cells. Cells are the basic unit of life, the smallest units that can carry out all the processes of life. This connects living things that look very different. Plants and animals are made of cells. So are bacteria and archaea. Their cells differ in size and shape, but cells are what they share.

scenes.visual: Move from plant and animal tissues to a bacterium and an archaeon. Highlight cells in every example. Display: "All living organisms are made of cells" and "Cells are the basic unit of life". Use varied cell shapes; remove the cork opening and historical-delay arrow.

scenes.tts: Every new cell comes from a cell that already existed. New cells form when existing cells divide. The cell theory connects living things through cells, and explains where new cells come from.

scenes.visual: Follow one existing cell as it divides into new cells. Label: "New cells arise from existing cells". Keep this division sequence available for the next scene.

scenes.tts: The cell theory has six ideas. The other three explain what cells do and share. Metabolism happens inside cells. These chemical reactions include breaking down sugar to release energy for the cell to use. D N A carries hereditary information. When a cell divides, each new cell gets a copy. Cells also share the same main kinds of molecules: proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids. The details differ, but the basic composition is shared.

scenes.visual: Develop the remaining three ideas around the same cell: sugar breakdown and energy use inside it; DNA copied and passed to new cells during division; shared molecular categories in differently shaped cells. Finish with six short labels, with the first three already established. Do not imply identical cell composition in every detail.

scenes.tts: How did scientists support these ideas? Hooke's cork showed walls of dead cells in one plant material. Scientists had to compare many plant and animal tissues to find the shared cellular plan. They also corrected a wrong idea: that new cells could form inside a structureless fluid. Remak published evidence that existing cells divide. Virchow spread the idea: every cell comes from a cell. A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation supported by many lines of evidence. It can change when new evidence arrives.

Cross out the fluid-to-new-cell model; replace it with Remak's division evidence and Virchow's statement. End on "Theory: a well-tested explanation". Remove chronology-led staging and dates; the comparison and correction carry the scene.

scenes.tts: Microscopes helped reveal the evidence. Magnification makes an image bigger. Resolution decides how much detail it holds. Enlarging a blur cannot add missing detail. Many cells are almost clear. Stains add contrast by sticking to some parts more than others.

scenes.visual: Magnify an unresolved pair of points: the blur grows without separating. Improve resolution to show the pair. Then show an almost clear cell and add stain so its nucleus stands out. Keep resolution and contrast as distinct effects.

scenes.tts: An ordinary light microscope can show a cheek cell or a bacterium. Ribosomes are too small for it to resolve. Electron microscopes reveal finer details, including ribosomes.

Replace the long numerical size ladder with this single tool-selection example. Do not suggest that magnifying a light-microscope image reveals ribosomes.

scenes.tts: Tools made observations possible. Comparisons and evidence of division supported and corrected the theory. Its central idea connects all living things: cells are the basic units of life.

Hold the closing cellular-unity image and fade out. No additional spoken claim.
